passages.t: ‘I waited patiently for the LORD’, and the miry clay
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David” (verse 1). He tells a story of rescue. “I waited patiently for the LORD; He inclined to me and heard my cry” (verse 1).

“He lifted me up from the pit of despair, out of the miry clay; He set my feet upon a rock, and made my footsteps firm” (verse 2). “He put a new song in my mouth, a hymn of praise to our God. Many will see and fear and put their trust in the LORD” (verse 3).

“Blessed is the man who has made the LORD his trust” (verse 4). And he cannot count all God has done: “Many, O LORD my God, are the wonders You have done” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
This is a song of thanks. ‘Waited patiently’ is in Hebrew a doubled verb, something like ‘I waited and waited’. The rescue did not come fast.

The pit and the clay come from the land. A pit could be a cistern, a deep hole cut in rock to store rainwater. When it was empty it held only mud at the bottom, and a person thrown in could sink and not climb out. That happened to the prophet Jeremiah: they lowered him into a cistern that had “no water but only mud, and Jeremiah sank down into the mud” (Jeremiah 38:6). ‘The pit of despair’ is a picture of being stuck, sinking, with no way up. Then God sets him on rock.

Notice the ‘new song’. Rescue gives him something new to sing, and others hear it and trust God too (verse 3). His story becomes theirs.
passages.later:
Jeremiah's cistern (Jeremiah 38:6) shows what the pit of verse 2 was like, and he was lifted out with ropes.

Revelation hears a ‘new song’ sung to the Lamb (Revelation 5:9). And Paul prays that the church may live in harmony, “so that with one mind and one voice you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 15:6): many voices joined in praise, as in verse 3.
passages.hard:
‘I waited patiently’ can sound as if the wait was easy. It was not. The doubled Hebrew verb stresses the waiting, and the psalm's last verse is still asking God ‘do not delay’ (verse 17).

If you are still in the pit, verse 1 does not tell you how long it will take. It tells you that someone else was there and was heard. If you feel stuck and sinking, please tell someone you trust. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
Where have you been lifted out of the mud? The psalm asks you to tell it, so that others ‘will see and fear and put their trust in the LORD’.

And if you are still waiting, it asks you to keep waiting on God, not on something that cannot hold your weight.

passages.t: ‘My ears You have opened’, and ‘Here I am, I have come’
passages.happening:
Then a surprising line. “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but my ears You have opened. Burnt offerings and sin offerings You did not require” (verse 6).

“Then I said, ‘Here I am, I have come” (verse 7), and he speaks of a scroll that is written about him: “I delight to do Your will, O my God; Your law is within my heart” (verse 8).

So he cannot keep quiet. “I proclaim righteousness in the great assembly; behold, I do not seal my lips” (verse 9). “I have not concealed Your loving devotion and faithfulness from the great assembly” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Verse 6 does not mean that God hated the sacrifices he had commanded. The prophets say the same kind of thing. Samuel told King Saul, “obedience is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22). Hosea says, “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6). An offering without a willing heart was empty.

‘My ears You have opened’ is in Hebrew ‘ears You have dug for me’. It probably means: You have given me ears that truly listen and obey. Some readers hear a link with the servant who chose to stay with his master for life and had his ear pierced at the doorpost (Exodus 21:6). The words are not the same, so that link is uncertain.

‘The scroll’ may be the book of God's law. Deuteronomy told Israel's king to write out his own copy of it (Deuteronomy 17:18). The speaker says: what is written there is about me; I am to live it.
passages.later:
Hebrews quotes verses 6 to 8 as the words of Christ coming into the world: “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me. In burnt offerings and sin offerings You took no delight. Then I said, ‘Here I am, it is written about Me in the scroll: I have come to do Your will, O God.’” (Hebrews 10:5-7). Hebrews then says that “by that will, we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:10).

Jesus himself prayed in Gethsemane, “Yet not as I will, but as You will” (Matthew 26:39).
passages.hard:
Hebrews has ‘a body You prepared for Me’, but the psalm in our Bible has ‘my ears You have opened’. Why the difference?

It is fair to state it plainly. The Hebrew text of the psalm says ‘ears You have dug for me’. The Greek translation of the Old Testament, which the writer of Hebrews used, reads ‘a body You prepared for me’ (some copies of the Greek have ‘ears’). No one knows for certain how the Greek reading arose. Hebrews quotes the Greek, as the New Testament writers often did.

Readers have answered in more than one way. Many point out that the two readings mean much the same: ears are part of a body, and both speak of a whole self given to God to obey. Others see in the Greek a fuller meaning that the writer of Hebrews drew out: the obedient Son took a human body and offered it. Hebrews' point does not depend on one word. It is that God wanted obedience more than animal sacrifices, and that Jesus gave it, in his body, once for all.
passages.asks:
‘Here I am’ is a short prayer that changes everything after it. The psalm asks whether you can say it about God's will today, before you know all of what it will cost.

It also asks what you keep quiet about. He ‘did not seal his lips’. Who needs to hear what God has done for you?

passages.t: ‘My sins have overtaken me’, and ‘O my God, do not delay’
passages.happening:
The mood changes again, and trouble returns. “O LORD, do not withhold Your mercy from me” (verse 11). “For evils without number surround me; my sins have overtaken me, so that I cannot see. They are more than the hairs of my head, and my heart has failed within me” (verse 12).

“Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me; hurry, O LORD, to help me” (verse 13). He prays that those who mock him will be put to shame (verses 14-15), and that all who seek God will say, “The LORD be magnified!” (verse 16).

The psalm ends still waiting. “But I am poor and needy; may the Lord think of me. You are my helper and deliverer; O my God, do not delay” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Verses 13 to 17 appear again, with small changes, as Psalm 70. The Psalms sometimes reuse a prayer this way; Psalm 53 repeats Psalm 14. Scholars differ on which came first.

Notice the order of the whole psalm. Thanks first (verses 1 to 10), then a new cry for help (verses 11 to 17). The rescue of the past does not mean there will be no trouble in the future. It gives him a reason to ask again.

‘Poor and needy’ (verse 17) does not only mean having no money. It means having no power to help yourself.
passages.later:
Jesus began his work in Nazareth by reading that he was sent “to preach good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18).

Hebrews, which reads verses 6 to 8 as words of Christ, does not quote verse 12. That verse is the voice of a sinner who needs mercy, and every reader can pray it.
passages.asks:
The psalm does not end with the problem solved. It ends with ‘do not delay’. You may pray the same way: thankful for past rescues and honest that you need another one.

And it asks you to call yourself what you are before God: ‘poor and needy’. That is not a failure. It is where help begins.
